# Purpose

The rare-joint registries list few models: 4–13 per registry for total ankle and total elbow. The largest model often holds 30–50% of all procedures. A registry mean is then partly the rate of that one model, which causes two problems:

1. **Self-masking.** A large model with a high rate pulls the mean towards itself and looks less extreme than it is.
2. **Masking of others.** A large model with a high rate raises the reference for every other model. Other poor performers can then sit inside the funnel. A large model with a *low* rate does the opposite and makes the others look worse.

This report tests how much each model drives its registry mean, using two leave-one-out methods. It then checks whether the models flagged as outliers change when the reference is recomputed without them.
It also compares control limits for **small-volume models**, where the normal approximation used so far is poorly calibrated. Many rare-joint models have fewer than 300 procedures.

The analysis is exploratory and **the app is not changed**. The decisions and their justifications are collected at the end ([Decisions](#decisions)).

## Supervisor guidance (2026-10) and how this report follows it {#guidance}

| Issue with low-volume implants (e.g. total elbow) | Guidance | Where it is addressed |
|---|---|---|
| **Few implants (n) per brand/type** | Use a **90%** confidence interval / control limit. It has been used in the literature, and a two-sided 90% limit is a one-sided 95% test, in line with non-inferiority testing. | Default flagging level is now `level` = `r level_label(P$level)`. The new section [Lower control limits for screening](#screening) compares 90%, 95% and 99.8% funnels, with power and false-alarm tables. |
| **Few brands/types (k)** | The mean can be biased upwards by the potential outlier(s), which can hide them. Use a less biased mean: a **leave-one-out analysis** as in meta-analysis (`metafor`), taking the **lowest** leave-one-out mean as the least biased. | The **lowest metafor leave-one-out mean** is now its own reference (`min_loo_re`) and is drawn in the screening funnels. The subtraction version is kept for comparison. See [references](#references). |

**Why a 90% limit is a one-sided 95% test.** A two-sided 90% limit leaves 5% of the reference distribution above the upper limit and 5% below the lower limit. Screening for *poor* performance only uses the upper limit, so a model above it is flagged by a one-sided test at α = 0.05. This is the same convention as a non-inferiority (or equivalence) comparison judged with a 90% CI. The usual 95% funnel corresponds to one-sided α = 0.025, and 99.8% to α = 0.001.

# Data and model inputs {#data}

```{r load}
cfg <- load_rare_config(".")
exts <- purrr::compact(purrr::map(stats::setNames(unlist(P$joints), unlist(P$joints)), ~ load_rare(P$data_dir, .x)))
runs <- purrr::map(exts, ~ loo_run(.x, cfg, T_YR, k_min = P$k_min, test = P$ma_test, scale = P$ma_scale))
runs <- purrr::compact(runs)
skipped <- purrr::imap_chr(runs, ~ paste(.x$skipped, collapse = ", "))
```

**Models.** These are the model rows used by the rare-joint funnels: the AOANJRR supplements (A15 ankle, ET6–ET8 elbow) and NJR (3.A4 ankle, 3.E8 elbow), with model names harmonised by `config/rare_device_families.csv`.
Registries with fewer than `r P$k_min` models, or none at all, are left out of the meta-analysis: `r paste(sprintf("%s: %s", names(skipped), ifelse(skipped == "", "none", skipped)), collapse = "; ")`. LROI publishes no model-level rates for these joints.

**Each model's estimate and its uncertainty.** The meta-analysis needs a variance for each model's rate. Published rates are Kaplan-Meier cumulative revision percentages, not simple counts, so the variance is taken from the **published 95% CI**. That CI already accounts for censoring and the number still at risk. The calculation is done on a transformed scale, $y_i = f(p_i)$, here the **`r SC$label`** scale (parameter `ma_scale`), with

$$SE_i = \frac{f(ucl_i) - f(lcl_i)}{2 \times 1.96}.$$

All pooled results (means, CIs, prediction intervals, leave-one-out means) are back-transformed to the proportion scale with $f^{-1}$ before they are shown or used as funnel references.

| Scale | $f(p)$ | Back-transform $f^{-1}(y)$ | Delta-method factor $f'(p)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Complementary log-log (primary) | $\log(-\log(1 - p)) = \log(-\log S)$ | $1 - \exp(-\exp(y))$ | $1 / [-(1-p)\log(1-p)]$ |
| Logit (sensitivity) | $\log(p / (1 - p))$ | $1 / (1 + e^{-y})$ | $1 / [p(1-p)]$ |

The complementary log-log scale is the primary scale because registries build their Kaplan-Meier CIs on it (the log(−log S) variance of Kalbfleisch & Prentice 2002, recommended by the International Prosthesis Benchmarking Working Group 2018, Recommendation 10). The published CIs are symmetric on that scale (median ratio of upper to lower half-width ≈ 1.00), so the SE read back is the registry's own. Heaps et al. (2019) pooled arthroplasty survival on this scale with REML in `metafor`. The logit scale, the usual scale for pooling proportions (Lin & Chu 2020), is run as a [sensitivity analysis](#scale-sensitivity); the two agree closely when event probabilities are low (Salika et al. 2022). Both keep pooled rates between 0 and 1 and allow for the asymmetric KM CIs on the percent scale.

* **AOANJRR elbow** stems are printed separately for fracture, OA and RA (ET6–ET8). As in the funnels, each stem's rows are pooled: the rate is n-weighted, and the SE is combined on the percent scale as $SE = \sqrt{\sum (w_j SE_j)^2}$ with $w_j = n_j / \sum n$, where each row's $SE_j$ is read from its own CI on the analysis scale and moved to the percent scale with the delta method, $SE_j = SE_{y,j} / f'(p_j)$. The SE is then moved to the analysis scale with the delta method, $SE_y = SE_p \times f'(p)$.
* **Fallback.** If a row has no usable CI or a 0% estimate, the code uses a binomial approximation with a 0.5 continuity correction. No row needs it at present.

```{r inputs}
purrr::map_dfr(runs, "models") |>
  left_join(tibble(joint = names(JOINT_NAME), joint_name = JOINT_NAME), by = "joint") |>
  arrange(joint, registry, desc(n_total)) |>
  transmute(joint = joint_name, registry, model, n = scales::comma(n_total),
            `share of registry n` = pct(share_n), rate = pct(p),
            `95% CI` = ifelse(is.na(lcl), sprintf("%s-%s", pct(SC$inv(yi - 1.96 * sei)), pct(SC$inv(yi + 1.96 * sei))),
                              sprintf("%s-%s", pct(lcl), pct(ucl))),
            SE = num(sei, 3), `SE source` = se_source,
            `few at risk` = ifelse(low_at_risk %in% TRUE, "yes", "")) |>
  rename(!!paste0("SE (", SCN, ")") := SE) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Model inputs at ", T_YR, " years"))
```

# How much does one model drive the mean? {#influence}

## Methods

**1. Subtraction leave-one-out.** This starts from the *published* registry mean $p_{pub}$ over all $N$ procedures, which includes the unlisted "other" models. It removes model $i$'s procedures:

$$p_{(-i)}^{sub} = \frac{N\,p_{pub} - n_i\,p_i}{N - n_i}$$

This is the mean the registry would report without model $i$, so it keeps the same *patient-weighted* estimand as the published mean: the expected rate for a typical **patient**.
It is an approximation. Kaplan-Meier rates do not add up exactly, because the models have different follow-up and censoring. It is the same approximation already used to pool rows in the funnels. No package is needed.

**2. Meta-analytic leave-one-out (`metafor`).**

* A **random-effects meta-analysis** of the model rates is fitted with `metafor::rma()`: `r SC$label` scale, REML estimate of the between-model variance $\tau^2$, and `r if (P$ma_test == "knha") "the Knapp-Hartung adjustment" else "z-based"` CI for the pooled mean.
* `metafor::leave1out()` refits the model $k$ times, each time leaving out one model.
* `influence()` returns the diagnostics described below.

The random-effects mean estimates the expected rate for a typical **model**, which is a different estimand from the published mean:

* **Weights.** Each model gets weight $w_i = 1/(v_i + \tau^2)$. When the models differ (large $\tau^2$), the weights move towards equal, so a model with 45% of the procedures may get only about 30% of the weight. That limits how far one model can drive the mean.
* **Common-effect mean.** Also shown for comparison, with $w_i = 1/v_i$ and no $\tau^2$. It is close to n-weighting.
* **Why Knapp-Hartung.** With $k$ = 4–13 models, the z-based CI of the pooled mean is too narrow. Knapp-Hartung uses a $t_{k-1}$ distribution and a rescaled variance, which gives better coverage when $k$ is small (IntHout et al. 2014, *BMC Med Res Methodol* 14:25).

## What the metrics mean {#metrics}

| Metric | What it is | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| **Share of n** | $n_i / N$ | How much of the registry the model is. |
| **Weight (CE / RE)** | Share of the inverse-variance weight in the common-effect (CE) and random-effects (RE) fits | RE weight < share of n means the meta-analysis limits the model's pull. |
| **$\tau^2$** | Between-model variance of the true rates on the `r SC$label` scale | 0 means the models differ only by chance. |
| **$I^2$** | Share of the total variation that is between models rather than sampling error | Roughly 25% = low, 50% = moderate, 75% = high heterogeneity. |
| **$Q$, p** | Cochran's test that all models share one rate | Low power with few models, so a non-significant Q does not show the models are the same. |
| **Prediction interval** | Where a new, typical model's rate is expected to fall (95%) | Wider than the CI of the mean. It is the meta-analytic counterpart of a funnel's width at very large n. |
| **Leave-one-out mean** | Pooled mean refitted without model $i$ (`leave1out()`) | How far the mean moves when the model is dropped. |
| **Externally standardised residual** (`rstudent`) | $z_i = (y_i - \hat\mu_{(-i)}) / \sqrt{v_i + \hat\tau^2_{(-i)} + \text{Var}(\hat\mu_{(-i)})}$ | The model compared with the mean of all **other** models, allowing for its own uncertainty, the heterogeneity and the uncertainty in that mean. It cannot mask itself. It is roughly N(0,1), so $|z| > 3.09$ corresponds to the 99.8% level. |
| **DFFITS** | Change in the pooled estimate when model $i$ is removed, in standard-error units | Large \|DFFITS\| means removing the model shifts the mean noticeably. |
| **Cook's distance** | Squared change in the pooled estimate when model $i$ is removed, scaled by the estimate's variance | Overall influence on the mean. metafor flags values above the median of $\chi^2_1$ (0.45). |
| **Covariance ratio** | Variance of the pooled estimate without model $i$ divided by with it | Below 1: removing the model makes the mean *more* precise, a sign of an outlier. |
| **Hat value** | The model's leverage, its share of the weight in the fit | Above $3/k$: the model alone holds a lot of the estimate. |
| **$\tau^2$ deleted** | $\tau^2$ refitted without model $i$ | A large drop means this model accounts for much of the heterogeneity. |
| **Influential (metafor rule)** | metafor's default flag (Viechtbauer & Cheung 2010, *Res Synth Methods* 1:112) | Flagged if any of: \|DFFITS\| > $3\sqrt{p/(k-p)}$; Cook's distance > median of $\chi^2_p$; hat > $3p/k$; or any DFBETAS > 1. Here $p = 1$ (intercept only). |

## Summary across follow-up years

```{r summary_years}
yrs_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(names(exts), function(j) purrr::map_dfr(unlist(P$time_yrs), function(t) {
  r <- loo_run(exts[[j]], cfg, t, k_min = P$k_min, test = P$ma_test, scale = P$ma_scale); if (is.null(r)) NULL else r$summary
}))
yrs_tbl |>
  left_join(tibble(joint = names(JOINT_NAME), joint_name = JOINT_NAME), by = "joint") |>
  arrange(joint, registry, time_yr) |>
  transmute(joint = joint_name, registry, years = time_yr, k,
            `published mean (95% CI)` = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", pct(p_pub, 0.01), pct(p_lcl), pct(p_ucl)),
            `leave-one-out range (subtraction)` = sprintf("%s-%s", pct(loo_sub_min, 0.01), pct(loo_sub_max, 0.01)),
            `outside published CI?` = ifelse(loo_sub_min < p_lcl | loo_sub_max > p_ucl, "yes", "no"),
            `RE mean (95% CI)` = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", pct(p_re, 0.01), pct(p_re_lb), pct(p_re_ub)),
            `leave-one-out range (RE)` = sprintf("%s-%s", pct(loo_re_min, 0.01), pct(loo_re_max, 0.01)),
            `I2` = paste0(round(I2), "%"),
            `largest model (share n / RE weight)` = sprintf("%s (%s / %s)", top_model, pct(top_share, 1), pct(top_w_re, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "How far the mean moves when one model is left out")
```

The **outside published CI?** column asks whether leaving out a single model moves the mean further than the registry's own 95% CI. If it does, the uncertainty in the reference from *which models are in the registry* is larger than its sampling uncertainty.

# Does the choice of reference change which models are flagged? {#references}

Each model is compared with six references. All use the same **`r P$limit_method`** control limits at the **`r level_label(LV)`** level, built around that reference and evaluated at the model's own n:

| Reference | Definition | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Published mean | The registry total, as in the funnels so far | Baseline |
| Own leave-one-out (subtraction) | The published total minus this model | Removes self-masking; same patient-weighted estimand |
| Random-effects mean | The meta-analytic mean of all models | Limits any one model's pull; model-weighted |
| Own leave-one-out (random effects) | The random-effects mean refitted without this model | Removes self-masking *and* limits the pull of the others |
| Lowest leave-one-out mean (subtraction) | The lowest subtraction leave-one-out mean in the registry | Least upward-biased patient-weighted mean |
| Lowest leave-one-out mean (random effects) | The lowest `metafor::leave1out()` mean in the registry | **Least upward-biased mean (supervisor guidance)**; used in the screening funnels |

**The lowest leave-one-out mean.** With few models, a potential outlier pulls the mean up and hides itself and others. The leave-one-out mean is recomputed $k$ times, once without each model. The **lowest** of these is the mean without the model that inflates it most, which makes it the least upward-biased reference available. Following the supervisor guidance, the metafor (random-effects) version is the primary choice. Its weights are also less dominated by the largest model.

Two points to keep in mind when interpreting it:

* If the registry has **no** true outlier, the lowest leave-one-out mean is still slightly below the true mean, because it is the minimum of $k$ values. It then flags a few more models high than the published mean would. For screening, that is the intended trade-off: missing a poor implant costs more than reviewing one that turns out fine.
* It is one reference for the whole registry, so the model whose removal gives the minimum is judged against a mean that excludes it. Every other model is judged against a mean that also excludes that model.

A model that is high against every reference, including the published mean, is the strongest signal. A model that is high only against the lowest leave-one-out mean is a screening signal worth reviewing, not a finding.

**How to read the figure.** Each row of panels is one reference; each column is one registry.

* **Point:** the model's rate minus its reference. Zero means the model is exactly at its reference.
* **Bracket (vertical bar at the point):** that model's own upper and lower control limit at its own n. A point outside its bracket is flagged. The brackets are the actual test.
* **Grey funnel:** drawn only where **every model in the registry shares the same reference** (published mean, random-effects mean, both lowest leave-one-out means). A funnel is one curve built around one value, so it can only be drawn when there is one value.
* **No funnel in the "own leave-one-out" rows:** there, each model is compared with the mean of all the *other* models, so every model has a *different* reference (Coonrad-Morrey's mean excludes Coonrad-Morrey, Latitude's excludes Latitude, and so on). There would be one funnel per model, and drawing them all would be unreadable. The bracket is simply that model's own funnel, cut out at its own n.

In the shared-reference rows, the brackets sit exactly on the funnel, which is a check that the two agree.

```{r status, results = "asis", fig.width = 11, fig.height = 15}
status_all <- purrr::map_dfr(runs, ~ loo_status(.x, LV, P$limit_method))
for (j in names(runs)) {
  cat("\n\n## ", JOINT_NAME[[j]], "\n\n", sep = "")
  st <- filter(status_all, joint == j)
  p <- plot_loo_status(st, runs[[j]], P$x_log,
         title = paste0(JOINT_NAME[[j]], ", ", T_YR, " years: model status under each reference (", level_label(LV), ", ", P$limit_method, " limits)"),
         subtitle = "Point: model rate minus its own reference. Bracket: that model's own control limits. Grey funnel: shared reference",
         caption = "Labelled: models outside their limits.")
  print(p); save_fig(p, paste0(tolower(j), "_", T_YR, "yr_status_by_reference"), 11, 15)
}
```

```{r status_table}

status_all |>
  mutate(cell = paste0(c(above = "HIGH", within = "ok", below = "low")[as.character(status)], " (", pct(dev), ")")) |>

  arrange(joint, registry, desc(n_total)) |>
  transmute(joint = joint_name, registry, model, n = scales::comma(n_total),
            `published` = pub, `own LOO (subtr.)` = loo_sub, `RE mean` = re, `own LOO (RE)` = loo_re,
            `lowest LOO (subtr.)` = min_loo, `lowest LOO (RE)` = min_loo_re, `meta-analytic test (z)`) |>

                                "ok = within limits. The meta-analytic test is described in the next section."))
```

# Limits for small-volume models {#small-volume}

## Why the normal approximation fails at small n

So far the funnels have used normal limits by default, $p_0 \pm z\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$. For a binomial count, the normal approximation is poor when $n p_0$ is small, roughly below 10–20. At a 5% revision rate that is any model with fewer than about 200–400 procedures, which covers most rare-joint models:

* The binomial distribution is skewed to the right at low rates. Normal limits are symmetric, so the **upper limit is too low**: models are flagged high too often.
* The normal **lower limit** is often below 0 at small n (clipped to 0 in the plots), so a low outlier cannot be detected. This also happens with exact limits at very small n. There it is a real limitation of the data, not of the method: with a 5% rate and 50 procedures, zero revisions is still plausible.
* The **exact** limits (Spiegelhalter 2005, *Stat Med* 24:1185) use binomial quantiles, interpolated between whole counts so the funnel is smooth. They are better calibrated at small n and match the normal limits at large n.

The table shows how often each limit is actually exceeded by a model whose true rate *is* the reference (5%). The target for the `r level_label(LV)` level is `r (1 - LV) / 2 * 100`% on each side:

```{r calibration}
calib <- limit_calibration(0.05, c(25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 5000), LV)
calib |>
  transmute(n, method, `upper limit` = pct(upper), `lower limit` = pct(lower, 0.01),
            `P(above upper)` = sprintf("%.4f", p_above), `P(below lower)` = sprintf("%.4f", p_below),
            `x target (upper)` = sprintf("%.1f", p_above / target)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Calibration of the ", level_label(LV), " limits for a true rate of 5% (binomial)"))
```

The **x target (upper)** column shows how many times more often than intended a model with the reference rate is flagged high. The exact limits are never worse than the normal limits and are much closer to the target at most n (e.g. 1.2× vs 7.2× at n = 25; 1.5× vs 4.3× at n = 100). Where both are equally off (n = 50, 250), the two limits fall between the same two whole counts. With a discrete count, no limit can hit the target exactly; the interpolation is designed to be right on average, not at every n. The normal limits are 2–7 times too liberal below n ≈ 250.

```{r limit_methods, results = "asis", fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5.5}
for (j in names(runs)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", JOINT_NAME[[j]], ": normal vs exact limits\n\n", sep = "")
  p <- plot_limit_methods(runs[[j]], LV, P$x_log,
         title = paste0(JOINT_NAME[[j]], ", ", T_YR, " years: normal vs exact ", level_label(LV), " limits around the published mean"),
         subtitle = "The two sets of limits differ most at small n, where most rare-joint models are")
  print(p); save_fig(p, paste0(tolower(j), "_", T_YR, "yr_limit_methods"), 11, 5.5)
}
```

```{r normal_vs_exact}
purrr::map_dfr(runs, function(r) {
  bind_rows(mutate(loo_status(r, LV, "normal"), lim = "normal"), mutate(loo_status(r, LV, "exact"), lim = "exact"))
}) |>
  filter(ref == "pub") |>
  select(joint, registry, model, n_total, p, p0, lim, status) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = lim, values_from = status) |>
  filter(normal != exact) |>
  transmute(joint = JOINT_NAME[joint], registry, model, n = n_total, rate = pct(p), `published mean` = pct(p0, 0.01),
            `normal limits` = normal, `exact limits` = exact) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Models whose status (vs the published mean) differs between normal and exact limits")
```

If the table is empty, no model changes status at this year and level. The exact limits are still the safer default.

## The meta-analytic test: a third option for small volumes

The externally standardised residual from `influence()` (the `rstudent` column above) is an outlier test in its own right. It differs from a funnel in three ways that matter for small models:

1. **It uses each model's own published CI**, so it allows for censoring and the number still at risk. A binomial funnel uses only n and treats the KM percentage as if every patient had been followed for the full time.
2. **It compares the model with the mean of all other models**, so the model cannot mask itself.
3. **It allows for the real spread between models ($\tau^2$)**, so it is more conservative than a binomial funnel when the models genuinely differ. It is the meta-analytic counterpart of the overdispersed funnel.

Plotted against n, it is a flat funnel: the limits are ±`r num(qnorm(1 - (1 - LV) / 2))` for the `r level_label(LV)` level (solid) and ±1.96 for 95% (dashed).

```{r rstudent, results = "asis", fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5}
for (j in names(runs)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", JOINT_NAME[[j]], "\n\n", sep = "")
  p <- plot_rstudent(filter(rs_all, joint == j), LV, P$x_log,
         title = paste0(JOINT_NAME[[j]], ", ", T_YR, " years: leave-one-out standardised residuals"),
         subtitle = paste0("Each model vs the random-effects mean of the other models. Solid: ", level_label(LV), "; dashed: 95%"))
  print(p); save_fig(p, paste0(tolower(j), "_", T_YR, "yr_rstudent"), 11, 5)
}
```

**Funnel or meta-analytic test?** They answer slightly different questions:

* A **binomial funnel** asks whether the model is outside what chance alone would give *if it performed exactly like the reference*.
* The **meta-analytic test** asks whether the model is outside the range of *normal model-to-model variation*.

A model flagged by the funnel but not by the meta-analytic test is unusual compared with the average, but within the spread that other models also show. A model flagged by both is a strong signal.

# Lower control limits for screening (90% and 95%) {#screening}

## Why lower limits for low-volume implants

Funnel limits trade **false alarms** (flagging a model that performs like the reference) against **missed outliers** (not flagging a model that is worse). With large volumes, even a 99.8% limit catches a moderately worse implant. With the volumes typical of total elbows (often 100–500 per model), a 99.8% limit only catches implants that are dramatically worse, because the limit is far from the mean at small n.

For a screening tool, whose job is to say which implants to look at more closely, the balance should favour sensitivity. A 90% limit (one-sided α = 0.05, the non-inferiority convention) or a 95% limit (one-sided α = 0.025) does that. The supervisor guidance supports 90% for low-volume data. The same convention, a 90% CI read as a one-sided test, is used for non-inferiority in den Broeder et al. (2023), and 90% CIs are also used in orthopaedic cohort research (Groot et al. 2017) (see [References](#refs)).

## Power and false alarms

The table shows, for a reference rate of 5% (close to the 3-year rate for these joints) and `r P$limit_method` limits, the probability that a model is flagged high:

* **Power:** the probability of flagging a model whose true rate is 1.5×, 2× or 3× the reference.
* **False alarm:** the probability of flagging a model whose true rate *equals* the reference.

```{r power}
pw <- limit_power(0.05, c(1.5, 2, 3), c(50, 100, 250, 500, 1000), unlist(P$screen_levels), P$limit_method)
pw |>
  mutate(level = level_label(level), ratio = paste0(ratio, "x")) |>
  select(n, level, ratio, power, false_alarm) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = ratio, values_from = power, names_prefix = "power, true rate ") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !n, ~ sprintf("%.2f", .x))) |>
  rename(`false alarm (true rate = reference)` = false_alarm) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Probability of a high flag, reference rate 5% (binomial)")
```

Read across a row: at n = 250, a model with double the revision rate is caught most of the time at 90% and 95%, but noticeably less often at 99.8%. At n = 50–100, only the lower limits have useful power. The cost is the false-alarm column. At 90%, 5–10% of models that perform exactly like the reference are flagged high. That is the nominal 5% or a little above at small n, because revision counts are whole numbers and the limit falls between two counts. At 95% it is 3–4%, and at 99.8% almost 0. In a registry with $k$ models, about $0.05k$–$0.1k$ false high flags are expected at 90% (0.2–1.3 for $k$ = 4–13), and about $0.03k$ at 95% (0.1–0.5).

## Funnels at 90%, 95% and 99.8%

Each panel shows the 90%, 95% and 99.8% `r P$limit_method` limits around one reference: the published mean (top) and the lowest metafor leave-one-out mean (bottom). Points are coloured by the highest level whose limit they are outside.

```{r screen_funnels, results = "asis", fig.width = 11, fig.height = 8}
SL <- unlist(P$screen_levels)
screen_all <- purrr::map_dfr(runs, ~ screen_status(.x, SL, unlist(P$screen_refs), P$limit_method))
for (j in names(runs)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", JOINT_NAME[[j]], "\n\n", sep = "")
  ss <- filter(screen_all, joint == j)
  p <- plot_screen_funnels(ss, runs[[j]], SL, P$limit_method, P$x_log,
         title = paste0(JOINT_NAME[[j]], ", ", T_YR, " years: funnels at ", paste(level_label(sort(SL)), collapse = ", "), " limits"),
         subtitle = "Top: published mean. Bottom: lowest metafor leave-one-out mean (least upward-biased)",
         caption = paste0(P$limit_method, " binomial limits. Labelled: models outside at least the ", level_label(min(SL)), " limit."))
  print(p); save_fig(p, paste0(tolower(j), "_", T_YR, "yr_screen_funnels"), 11, 8)
}
```

```{r screen_counts}
screen_all |>
  tidyr::crossing(level = SL) |>
  group_by(joint, registry, ref, level) |>
  summarise(models = n(), high = sum(!is.na(above) & above >= level), low = sum(!is.na(below) & below >= level),
            flagged_high = paste(sort(model[!is.na(above) & above >= level]), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(joint = JOINT_NAME[joint], reference = LOO_REFS[as.character(ref)], level = level_label(level)) |>
  arrange(joint, registry, reference, level) |>
  select(joint, registry, reference, level, models, high, low, flagged_high) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Models above / below the limit at each level, by reference")
```

```{r screen_table}
screen_all |>
  select(joint, registry, model, n_total, p, ref, p0, screen) |>
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%s (ref %s)", screen, pct(p0, 0.01))) |>
  select(-p0, -screen) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = ref, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(joint, registry, desc(n_total)) |>
  mutate(joint = JOINT_NAME[joint], n_total = scales::comma(n_total), p = pct(p)) |>
  rename(n = n_total, rate = p) |>
  rename_with(~ LOO_REFS[.x], any_of(names(LOO_REFS))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Each model's screening status: the highest level whose limit it is outside")
```

**How to use this for screening.** Models outside the 90% limit against the lowest leave-one-out mean form the review list. Of those, models that are also outside against the published mean, at 95%, or on the meta-analytic test are the stronger signals. A model flagged only at 90% against the lowest leave-one-out mean is the weakest signal: worth a look, and a reason to recheck at the next report year.

# Sensitivity: complementary log-log vs logit scale {#scale-sensitivity}

```{r scale_cmp, eval = isTRUE(P$scale_compare)}
SCALE_CMP <- loo_scale_compare(exts, cfg, unlist(P$time_yrs), scales = c(P$ma_scale, SC_OTHER), k_min = P$k_min,
                               test = P$ma_test, level = LV, method = P$limit_method)
SCALE_W <- loo_scale_wide(SCALE_CMP, P$ma_scale, SC_OTHER)
```

The meta-analysis was refitted on the `r MA_SCALES[[SC_OTHER]]$label` scale, with each SE taken from the same published CI on that scale. The table compares the random-effects mean, the lowest leave-one-out mean (and the model it leaves out) and the models flagged against that mean (`r scales::percent(LV)` `r P$limit_method` limits). $\tau^2$ is in each scale's own units.

```{r scale_table, eval = isTRUE(P$scale_compare)}
SCALE_CMP |>
  arrange(joint, registry, time_yr, factor(scale, levels = c(P$ma_scale, SC_OTHER))) |>
  transmute(joint = JOINT_NAME[joint], registry, years = time_yr, scale, k,
            `RE mean (95% CI)` = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", pct(p_re, 0.01), pct(p_re_lb), pct(p_re_ub)),
            `95% prediction interval` = sprintf("%s-%s", pct(pi_lb), pct(pi_ub)),
            tau2 = num(tau2, 3), I2 = paste0(round(I2), "%"),
            `lowest LOO mean` = pct(loo_re_min, 0.01), `left out` = drop_for_min_re,
            `flagged vs lowest LOO` = ifelse(flagged == "", "none", flagged)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Random-effects results on the two scales, by follow-up year (metafor rma, leave1out)")
```

```{r scale_agree, results = "asis", eval = isTRUE(P$scale_compare)}
none <- function(x) ifelse(x == "", "none", x)
cat("\n\n**Agreement.** Across ", nrow(SCALE_W), " registry-by-year fits, the random-effects means differ by at most ",
    sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(SCALE_W$d_re_pp))), " percentage points and the lowest leave-one-out means by at most ",
    sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(SCALE_W$d_loo_pp))), " points. The same model gives the lowest leave-one-out mean in ",
    sum(SCALE_W$same_drop), " of ", nrow(SCALE_W), " fits, and the same models are flagged in ",
    sum(SCALE_W$same_flags), " of ", nrow(SCALE_W), ".", sep = "")
dis <- dplyr::filter(SCALE_W, !same_drop | !same_flags)
if (nrow(dis)) {
  cat(" Where they differ:\n\n")
  flag_txt <- ifelse(dis$same_flags, "; flags identical",
                     paste0("; flags ", none(dis$flagged_a), " vs ", none(dis$flagged_b)))
  cat(paste0("* ", JOINT_NAME[dis$joint], " ", dis$registry, ", ", dis$time_yr, " years: lowest LOO leaves out ",
             dis$drop_for_min_re_a, " (", pct(dis$loo_re_min_a, 0.01), ", ", P$ma_scale, ") vs ",
             dis$drop_for_min_re_b, " (", pct(dis$loo_re_min_b, 0.01), ", ", SC_OTHER, ")", flag_txt),
      collapse = "\n")
}
cat("\n\n")
```

# Decisions and justifications {#decisions}

| # | Decision | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Analyse total ankle and total elbow, AOANJRR and NJR only | These are the registries with model-level rates. LROI has none for these joints. The UKA registries have many models and large n, so one model drives the mean much less (can be run later with the same functions). |
| 2 | Model variance from the **published KM 95% CI**, on the **complementary log-log** scale; logit as a sensitivity analysis | Accounts for censoring and the number at risk, which a binomial variance from n does not. Registries compute KM CIs on the log(−log S) scale (Kalbfleisch & Prentice 2002; Benchmarking Working Group 2018), so the SE read back from the CI is the registry's own; the same scale was used for pooling UKA survival by Heaps et al. (2019). The logit refit (Lin & Chu 2020) checks that results do not depend on the choice ([sensitivity](#scale-sensitivity)). All results are back-transformed to the proportion scale. |
| 3 | AOANJRR elbow stems pooled across diagnoses, SE by n-weighted combination + delta method | Matches the rare-joint funnels (one point per stem). Leaving out a stem must drop all its diagnosis rows together. |
| 4 | Two leave-one-out methods: **subtraction** and **random-effects (`metafor::leave1out`)** | Subtraction keeps the published, patient-weighted estimand and the unlisted models. The random-effects version also limits the pull of the other large models, through more equal weights. |
| 5 | REML $\tau^2$ with **Knapp-Hartung** CIs; a common-effect fit only for comparison | REML is the recommended $\tau^2$ estimator. Knapp-Hartung gives better coverage of the pooled mean with few models (IntHout et al. 2014). The common-effect fit shows how much the n-dominant model would drive an inverse-variance mean. |
| 6 | Influence diagnostics and the "influential" flag from `metafor::influence()` defaults | A standard, citable rule (Viechtbauer & Cheung 2010) rather than our own cut-offs. |
| 7 | The **lowest leave-one-out mean** (metafor, random effects) is a reference in its own right and is used in the screening funnels; the subtraction version is kept for comparison | Supervisor guidance: with few models, the mean is biased upwards by potential outliers, and the lowest leave-one-out mean is the least biased. It is slightly low when there is no outlier, which suits screening (sensitivity over specificity). Models high against every reference remain the strongest signals. |
| 8 | **Exact** binomial limits (Spiegelhalter 2005) for the reference comparisons | Normal limits flag models with the reference rate several times too often below n ≈ 250 (calibration table), and their lower limit is often below 0. Exact limits match the normal ones at large n, so nothing is lost for large models. |
| 9 | The meta-analytic leave-one-out residual (`rstudent`) shown as a third flagging method | It uses each model's own CI, cannot mask itself, and allows for real between-model variation. It is the most defensible single test for few, small models. |
| 11 | Default flagging level **90%** (`level`), with 95% and 99.8% compared in the screening section | Supervisor guidance for low-volume implants. A two-sided 90% limit is a one-sided 95% test, the non-inferiority convention (den Broeder et al. 2023; 90% CIs also in Groot et al. 2017). Power at n = 50–500 is much higher than at 99.8%, at the cost of about 1 false high flag per 10–20 models that perform like the reference. |
| 10 | Only the report is changed; the app is unchanged | Exploratory. The choice of default reference and limits for the app should wait until these results have been reviewed. |

# Caveats {#caveats}

* **Few models.** With $k$ = 4–5 (elbow), $\tau^2$ is estimated imprecisely and can be 0 by chance. Influence statistics are unstable, because removing one model removes 20–25% of the data. Treat elbow results as illustrative.
* **Two estimands.** The published and subtraction means are patient-weighted (a typical patient). The random-effects means are model-weighted (a typical model). Both are reasonable benchmarks, but they answer different questions. A model can be "average for its patients" and still sit high among the models.
* **KM rates are not additive.** The subtraction method treats the published rate as an n-weighted average of the models' rates, which is approximately but not exactly true.
* **Binomial funnels ignore censoring.** The exact limits fix the small-n approximation, but they still treat the KM percentage as a proportion of n. The meta-analytic test uses the published CIs and avoids this. This is one reason to give it weight.
* **Multiple comparisons.** Each registry is tested several times (6 references × several models). At 90%, about 1 in 10–20 models with the reference rate is flagged high by chance. This is acceptable for screening, but the flags are hypotheses to review, not findings.
* **Different populations.** AOANJRR ankle models (A15) and the A11 mean cover all diagnoses. NJR elbow models are total elbows (trauma + elective). These match the scope decisions in the main README.

# References {#refs}

**Use of 90% confidence intervals** (supervisor guidance; justification for the 90% screening limit):

* den Broeder N, den Broeder AA, Verhoef LM, van den Hoogen FHJ, van der Maas A, van den Bemt BJF. Non-medical switching from tocilizumab to sarilumab in rheumatoid arthritis patients with low disease activity, an observational study. *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2023;114(4):810–814. doi:10.1002/cpt.2999. Its co-primary outcomes are judged by the **90% CI** against a non-inferiority margin, i.e. a one-sided test at α = 0.05, the same logic as a 90% upper funnel limit.
* Groot JAM, Jonkers FJ, Kievit AJ, Kuijer PPFM, Hoozemans MJM. Beneficial and limiting factors for return to work following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a retrospective cohort study. *Arch Orthop Trauma Surg* 2017;137(2):155–166. doi:10.1007/s00402-016-2594-6. An orthopaedic cohort study that reports **90% confidence intervals**.

**Methods**

* Lin L, Chu H. Meta-analysis of proportions using generalized linear mixed models. *Epidemiology* 2020;31(5):713–717. doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001232.
* Salika T, Turner RM, Fisher D, Tierney JF, White IR. Implications of analysing time-to-event outcomes as binary in meta-analysis: empirical evidence from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. *BMC Med Res Methodol* 2022;22:73. doi:10.1186/s12874-022-01541-9.
